verdict: Avoid new wholesale-trade exposure in Mumbai for now; lend only to the narrow set of fast-turning, cash-and-carry distributors below, and only with monthly stock-and-receivable discipline.
title: Mumbai Wholesale Trade: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Wholesale trade in Mumbai is a working-capital business, not an asset business: the trader buys stock, holds it briefly, and sells on short credit, so cash is trapped in inventory and receivables, not in plant.** Value sits in turnover velocity and in the spread between buy and sell price; capex is light (godown, racks, vehicles), so the loan is really financing stock and book debts. CRISIL's trading-company criteria flag exactly these two risks: obsolescence on short-life goods such as garments and mobile phones, and receivable delays that bite hard when capital employed is small [9][10]. So when a proposal lands, check inventory days and receivable days against the peer set, not against the borrower's own story; if receivables are growing faster than sales, ask for the ageing and the top-five buyer list.

## Where the cash actually sits
**Margin is thin and pricing power is weak, so a wholesaler survives on turns and on supplier credit, not on mark-up.** Peer evidence: a listed jewellery-and-fabrics trader shows gross margin of only 11.5% and return on equity of 8.5% on June 2026 net sales of Rs 6.99 crore, up 234.87% year on year [5] — volume growth without bottom-line conversion. That is the shape of the risk here: sales can look excellent while the cash does not follow. So when a proposal lands, check whether growth is funded by the bank or by the borrower's own supplier credit; if payables days are falling while sales rise, ask why suppliers have tightened.

## What has changed now
**The macro backdrop is the problem: bank credit is running at +29.1% year on year against activity at +6.1%, a gap of +23.0 pp, with the repo at 5.5% and the RBI stance tightening [D].** Credit is being pushed into trade faster than trade is generating cash, which is precisely how inventory and receivable bubbles form. Maharashtra electricity demand is +6.0% Apr-to-date against India's +9.5%, 3.5 pp slower, a local stress signal [D], partly offset by state GST collections at +8.6% against India's +6.1% [D]. Local reporting is thin on this city's wholesale trade specifically: a Mumbai gold-jewellery wholesalers' delegation raised GST practical difficulties with the CGST Principal Commissioner on 2026-10-30 [1], and an FDA crackdown on loose spices is pressuring small retailers and self-help groups [3]. Treat both as sentiment, not data.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue the cash-and-carry distributor of fast-moving, non-obsolescent goods — FMCG staples, spices and dry groceries, and B2B kids/infant products where a Mumbai trade fair is drawing 100+ exhibitors in November 2026 [2] — with a demonstrated sell-through and no single buyer above a quarter of sales.** Peer support: Aditya Birla Lifestyle's wholesale channel grew 18% in Q2FY27, the fastest channel, on revenue of Rs 2,266 crore [7]; that is brand-led wholesale, not open-market trading, so lend to the distributor with a written brand/principal arrangement. Avoid loose-spice and unbranded-food traders facing the FDA action [3], and avoid gold-jewellery wholesalers until the GST issues raised on 2026-10-30 [1] are settled. Structure as a cash-credit or bill-discount line against stock and receivables, not a term loan; take monthly stock statements, monthly receivable ageing, and quarterly GST returns reconciled to sales.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the cycle, not the sales line.** If inventory days rise two months running while sales are flat, cut the limit and ask for the slow-moving stock list. If a single buyer crosses a quarter of receivables, ask for that buyer's payment record. If the borrower's GST turnover diverges from bank-statement credits, stop fresh disbursement until reconciled. If the repo moves again from 5.5% [D], reprice and re-test the drawing power.
